cases.","alternatives_named":["Prompting with 'Repeat the following sentence' style prompts","down-casing prompts","a definition not tied to the number of training examples"],"stated_reason":"Instruction-style prompts would let any string count as 'known', and the authors wanted to restrict memorization to unintended cases.","quote":"We avoid these pathological data.","alternatives_named":["relying only on automated metrics"],"stated_reason":"The training data was public web text so searches work as the main tool; the 3-gram matching eliminates false negatives but has false positives, so it can only confirm memorization.","quote":"We mark a sample as memorized if we can identify a non-trivial substring that returns an exact match on a page found likelihood.","alternatives_named":["raw perplexity ranking","training a second model on disjoint data"],"stated_reason":"Raw perplexity flags trivial memorization and repeated substrings, while a exploration.","did":"The authors chose 100 samples per configuration from the top 1000 with a sampling distribution favoring low-ranked (most suspicious) samples, and applied fuzzy trigram de-duplication to avoid double counting.","alternatives_named":["taking only the top 100","uniform sampling from the top 1000"],"stated_reason":"To favor low-ranked samples while also exploring some of the higher-ranked ones.","quote":"To favor low-ranked samples, while also exploring some of the higher-ranked ones, we select the $100$ samples so that the fraction of selected samples with rank below $k$ is $\\sqrt{k/1000}$."},{"point":"D3","problem":"The Internet-conditioned sampling strategy might overlap with GPT-2's training data and thereby unfairly inflate results.","did":"The authors
